claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On the Imperfection of the Geological Record
claims.label: Extinct intermediates connect each species to a common progenitor, not to each other
claims.statement: The extinct intermediate forms required by descent with modification link each species to a common, usually unknown, progenitor, and that progenitor will generally have differed in some respects from all of its modified descendants, so forms directly intermediate between two living species should not be expected.

operationalizations.text: In morphological character spaces (PCA or phylogenetic morphospaces) combining extant clades (e.g., Equus vs. Tapirus, or pigeons) and their stem fossils, test whether reconstructed common ancestors and stem fossils lie at ancestral nodes exhibiting mosaic/plesiomorphic character combinations rather than on the direct Euclidean line segment connecting two extant crown species.

For related living species, infer their common ancestor on independent phylogenies and test whether fossil or reconstructed intermediates lie along separate stem lineages rather than morphologically midway between the living tips. The predicted branching pattern supports the claim.

In well-fossilized clades, place fossils and reconstructed ancestors in morphospace relative to living species pairs. Ancestors and fossils that lie off the straight line between two living species, and that connect each species to an earlier node, support the prediction; a surplus of fossils that are direct morphological intermediates between living species would count against it.

obstacles: Morphospace geometry depends on character selection and scaling, though discrete character polarity (plesiomorphy vs. synapomorphy) unambiguously distinguishes stem progenitors from direct crown-to-crown intermediates.
True ancestors are rarely identifiable as such.
Fossil sampling is uneven.
Multidimensional morphology makes 'directly intermediate' ambiguous.
Only clades with dense fossils and coded characters can be used.
Unequal rates of change move ancestors off the midpoint even when the path was a direct bridge.

claims.label: Species of large genera cluster unequally around certain species
claims.statement: Species of large genera are not equally distinct from one another but are clustered in little groups around certain other species, as varieties are clustered around their parent species.

operationalizations.text: Test tree imbalance (Colless's index, Sackin's index, beta-splitting parameter) and pairwise distance clustering (variance of nearest-neighbor distances or ultrametricity deviations) within large genera against a uniform/equidistant null model.

Quantify imbalance and multimodality of within-genus phylogenetic or phenotypic distances in large genera against equal-dispersion null models. Recurrent tight subclusters around central or ancestral forms support the claim.

Measure clustering of species around a few centers inside large genera, using morphological nearest-neighbour structure or phylogenetic satellites around paraphyletic nominal species, and compare that clustering with a constant-rate branching null. Excess clustering around a few species would support the satellite pattern; distances as even as the null would count against it.

obstacles: Incomplete taxon sampling in very large genera can bias tree imbalance statistics if sampling is non-random.
A 'central species' needs an explicit definition.
Taxonomic splitting itself creates clusters.
Ordinary branching processes already produce clusters, so the null has to be explicit.
Satellite species around a still-living 'parent' require paraphyletic species concepts that many trees have already removed.
Morphological clustering and phylogenetic clustering answer different versions of the statement.

claims.label: Sterility of first crosses differs from sterility of hybrids
claims.statement: The sterility of first crosses between pure species, whose reproductive organs are perfect, is a different phenomenon from the sterility of their hybrids, whose reproductive organs are functionally impotent.

operationalizations.text: Compare gamete/gonad functionality in pure parental species undergoing heterospecific crosses (measuring prezygotic pollen-pistil/sperm-egg barriers and F1 seed/zygote set) against gonad development, meiotic pairing, and gamete viability (pollen stainability, sperm motility, ovarian development) in the resulting F1 hybrids across plant and animal species pairs.
Separate fertilization or F1-production success from fertility of surviving F1 hybrids and compare their physiological causes. Distinct failure stages and mechanisms support the claimed distinction.

For species pairs, separate failure to produce offspring when parental gametogenesis is normal from sterility of F1 hybrids whose own gametogenesis fails. A systematic difference in the stage of failure supports two phenomena; a single shared stage of reproductive collapse would count against the distinction.

obstacles: In some crosses, F1 inviability (embryo lethality) prevents measuring F1 reproductive organ function, requiring the comparison to focus on crosses that produce viable F1 adults.
Crossing records are dispersed and taxonomically biased.
Outside Drosophila, crossing tables that record the stage of failure are scattered in papers.
The distinction is close to a definition by stage, so some of the result is built into the scoring.
Plants and non-fly animals in the stated scope are poorly represented in the open compilation.

claims.label: North American and European temperate biotas share ancestry from Pliocene circumpolar land
claims.statement: The relationship, with very little identity, between the temperate inhabitants of North America and Europe arises because a common biota inhabited the nearly continuous circumpolar land in warmer Pliocene times and then migrated southward, becoming separated and modified on each continent.

operationalizations.text: Estimate divergence times and ancestral geographic ranges for disjunct temperate sister clades between North America and Eurasia using dated molecular phylogenies, and cross-check against high-latitude Neogene/Pliocene fossil floras and faunas around the North Atlantic and Beringia.

Infer divergence times and ancestral ranges for temperate sister lineages in North America and Europe, and compare them with Pliocene circumpolar fossils and paleogeography. Support requires northern ancestral ranges and separation dates consistent with southward migration and Atlantic isolation.

Estimate divergence times and ancestral areas for temperate clades shared by North America and Europe, and check Pliocene fossils from Arctic landmasses. Divergences much older than the Pliocene, or no northern fossil connection, would count against this history.

obstacles: Much of the boreotropical and Arcto-Tertiary exchange occurred in the Eocene-Miocene rather than strictly the Pliocene, though Beringian exchange continued into the Pliocene.
Divergence-time uncertainty often spans multiple climatic episodes.
Different clades crossed via different routes and times.
Clock dates for the same clade often span more than the Pliocene.
A Beringian route and a North Atlantic route both fit a circumpolar source.
Very little identity has no sharp similarity threshold.

claims.label: Few living species will leave descendants; common species of dominant groups will prevail
claims.statement: Very few living species will leave descendants in the far future, and those that will prevail and give rise to new dominant species will be the common, widespread species of the larger, dominant groups.

operationalizations.text: Treat historical geological time bins in the fossil record as retrospective 'presents' and test whether: (1) only a small fraction of species in bin t leave descendant lineages surviving to bin t + k, and (2) species with wide geographic occupancy, high abundance (occurrence frequency), and membership in speciose higher taxa have significantly higher long-term survival and descendant diversification.

In fossil intervals, treat species present at an earlier time as the prediction cohort and test whether initially common, widespread species in species-rich clades disproportionately persist or give rise to later diversity. Low descendant survival overall and positive effects of abundance, range and clade dominance support the claim.

At successive fossil time slices, score which species or genera still have descendants several intervals later, and test whether survivorship and later diversification are concentrated in taxa that were common, widespread and members of already large groups. The claim is confirmed if those traits predict leaving descendants and most taxa leave none, and refuted if rare members of small groups persist as often as common members of dominant groups.

obstacles: Wide geographic range and high abundance also increase fossil sampling probability, so capture-mark-recapture (CMR / PyRate) models must be used to separate true survival and speciation from preservation bias.
Mass extinction events (e.g. K-Pg) sometimes eliminate dominant, speciose clades despite wide species ranges, altering background selectivity rules.
Direct ancestor-descendant links are rarely known.
Observed abundance and range are highly sampling-dependent.
The far future of living species is not directly testable.
Widespread taxa are more likely to be collected again, which imitates higher survivorship.
True species-level ancestor-descendant links are usually unavailable, so the test is forced down to genus occupancy.
Later geological intervals are a proxy for the 'far future', and the length of that proxy changes the result.

claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.label: Descent with divergence and extinction produces groups subordinate to groups
claims.statement: The nested arrangement of organisms into groups within groups (species within genera, genera within families, and so on) results from the modified descendants of a single progenitor diverging in character while less divergent forms are exterminated.

operationalizations.text: Compare morphological disparity matrices of extant clades against the same clades including extinct stem/intermediate fossils, testing whether hierarchical clustering structure (cophenetic correlation and gap statistics) becomes significantly more nested and discrete when extinct intermediates are removed.

Quantify hierarchical phylogenetic structure and compare diversification models with descent, trait divergence and extinction against models lacking those processes. Support requires nested monophyletic clusters and model evidence that divergence plus lineage loss generated observed gaps.

Ask whether character data from living and fossil organisms fit a branching hierarchy better than non-hierarchical or highly reticulate alternatives, and whether extinction of intermediate branches is required to reproduce the observed gaps between named groups. The claim is confirmed if tree-like structure is strong and simulated divergence without extinction of intermediates fails to produce the observed rank gaps, and refuted if the data are poorly hierarchical or gaps arise without that extinction.

obstacles: Any purely branching birth-death process automatically produces a tree topology, so separating selective extermination of intermediates from neutral stochastic extinction requires testing whether morphologically intermediate lineages go extinct at higher rates.
Fossil morphological matrices cover only skeletal/hard-part characters for a subset of clades.
Nestedness partly follows from tree-based representation.
Extinction histories are incomplete and alternative diversification processes can yield similar patterns.
A pure branching process produces nested groups even when extinction is random, so the specific role of exterminating less divergent forms is hard to isolate.
Building a tree and then reading nested groups off it is circular unless the test is a fit comparison against non-tree models.
Horizontal transfer, hybridization and uneven fossil recovery all reduce the clarity of the hierarchy.

claims.label: Competitors decline poleward, so climate acts more directly there
claims.statement: The number of species, and therefore of competitors, decreases going northward, so that going north or up a mountain one more often finds stunted forms caused by the direct harmful action of climate than going south or downhill.

operationalizations.text: Test across latitudinal and elevational transects whether local species richness declines poleward/upward while the frequency of dwarfed/stunted growth forms (e.g., krummholz, cushion plants, low canopy height relative to species potential) and abiotic vs biotic range-limit sensitivity increase.

Along replicated latitude and elevation gradients, test whether species richness declines and whether organism size or performance is more directly predicted by climate where competitor richness is low. The full linked pattern supports the claim.

Measure species richness along latitude and elevation, and measure the frequency of stunted individuals, asking whether stunting tracks direct climate stress more strongly poleward and uphill than equatorward and downhill, after accounting for season length and soil. A steeper richness decline and a higher share of climate-limited stunting toward the poles and summits would support the statement; stunting that is equally common in benign climates, or richness that does not decline, would count against it.

obstacles: Stunted stature at high latitudes and elevations is partly an adaptive genetically fixed strategy against wind/freezing rather than solely a direct plastic injury from harsh climate.
Trait data access and coverage are uneven.
Latitude, elevation and climate covary with productivity and history.
Short stature can be an adaptation to season length or nutrients rather than direct climatic injury.
Richness declines are real and still have many causes, so they do not by themselves show fewer competitors.
Tropical and high-elevation plot coverage is uneven, which can exaggerate apparent stunting.

claims.label: Races differ most in the parts man selects
claims.statement: Continued selection of slight variations in one part valued by man, such as leaves, flowers or fruit, produces races that differ from each other chiefly in that part, while other parts differ only slightly.

operationalizations.text: Calculate between-variety variance (or Qst / morphological disparity) of harvested target organs (e.g., fruit in gooseberries/tomatoes, leaves in cabbages, tubers in potatoes) versus non-targeted vegetative/floral organs across cultivars of the same species.

For crop varieties grouped by documented selection target, compare among-race standardized divergence in selected organs with divergence in unselected organs. Predominantly greater divergence in the selected part supports the rule; comparable divergence elsewhere refutes it.

For cultivated species, partition among-variety trait variance into the organ that breeders selected (leaf, flower, or fruit) and organs that were not the target. A larger share of variance in the selected organ would support the rule; similar variance in selected and unselected organs would refute it.

obstacles: Allometric scaling and pleiotropy cause some correlated divergence in unselected plant organs.
Phenotyping protocols differ among collections.
Correlated traits may blur organ-specific effects.
Genebank descriptors are often categorical, missing, and not measured with a common protocol.
Correlation of growth predicts that selected organs will drag others along, which shrinks the expected contrast.
The identity of the historically selected organ is uncertain for many old landraces.

claims.label: Parts repeated many times in an individual are variable in number
claims.statement: When a part or organ is repeated many times in one individual, such as snake vertebrae or stamens of polyandrous flowers, its number is variable, whereas parts present in small numbers are constant in number.

operationalizations.text: Compute intraspecific variance, standard deviation, and coefficient of variation in meristic counts (e.g. vertebral counts in snakes vs mammals/geckos; stamen and petal counts across oligandrous vs polyandrous angiosperms) and regress intraspecific variability against mean meristic count.

Across species, estimate within-species variance in part number and regress it on mean repeat number, comparing serial structures with low-copy homologues. A robust positive relationship and near constancy at low copy number support the claim.

Compare coefficients of variation in counts of many-times-repeated parts, such as vertebrae or stamens, with counts of parts that occur in small numbers. A decline in variability as the typical count declines would confirm the rule; similar coefficients after equalizing sample size would refute it.

obstacles: Must test both absolute variance and mean-scaled variance (coefficient of variation or developmental error scaling) so that the pattern is evaluated beyond trivial Poisson scaling.
Repositories emphasize species representatives rather than within-species samples.
Developmental constraints differ among structure types.
Within-species count variances are incomplete outside fishes and a subset of flowers.
Low-count parts are often defined as invariant, which can bake in the pattern.
Museum counts and trait databases use inconsistent sample sizes.

claims.label: Selection makes organisms only as perfect as their local competitors
claims.statement: Natural selection only makes each organism as perfect as, or slightly more perfect than, the other inhabitants of its own country, so endemic species of a region such as New Zealand may yield to species introduced from a larger region.

operationalizations.text: Test for asymmetry in naturalization success, population displacement, and extinction risk between continental introductions to islands (such as New Zealand) and island-to-continent introductions, controlling for propagule pressure and human habitat disturbance.

Compare establishment, displacement, abundance, and performance of introduced versus endemic species across islands and continents while controlling for propagule pressure and environment. Systematic competitive replacement supports the prediction; endemic superiority under matched conditions opposes it.

Compare establishment and impact of species moved from larger biotas into smaller ones, including islands such as New Zealand, with the reverse direction. Systematic yielding of local endemics to invaders from richer biotas supports the biogeographic prediction; equal or reversed success would count against it.

obstacles: Higher invasion impact on islands is confounded by human land-use change, differential propagule pressure (trade asymmetry), and release from coevolved continental enemies rather than intrinsic competitive superiority alone.
Propagule pressure and human disturbance confound competitive superiority.
'Perfect' has no single measurable scale.
Invasion success is confounded by propagule pressure, disturbance, and enemy release, not only relative perfection.
'As perfect as local competitors' is not itself a measured variable; establishment is a proxy.
GloNAF covers plants, while the claim is about inhabitants in general.
